questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Incitement and the imminence test
questions.learningObjective: state the elements of the test that governs punishable incitement
questions.stem: A speaker addresses an assembled crowd and urges them to take part in a violent breach of the law the following week. Which test decides whether that speech may be punished?

options.text: Whether the speaker intended to cause imminent lawless action and whether the audience was likely to act on it
Whether the words were printed, broadcast from a loudspeaker, or simply spoken aloud to the crowd
options.misconception: believes the medium of the speech settles punishability

options.text: Whether the crowd actually carried out the breach the following week before the speech can be punished
options.misconception: believes a completed breach is a precondition of liability

options.text: Whether the speaker was paid to appear or had travelled to the city in order to deliver the address
options.misconception: believes payment or travel bears on the test

questions.explanation: Speech is protected unless it falls within a category the law has excepted, and the excepted category of incitement is drawn narrowly: the government must show that the speaker intended to encourage an imminent lawless act and that the audience was likely to act on the encouragement. Imminence is what separates advocacy of a crime from advocacy of protest, and a demand for action now reads differently from a description of what ought to happen eventually. The medium, the speaker's payment, and whether the crowd later acted are all beside the point, because a speech that falls short of the test is protected whatever channel carries it and whatever follows.

questions.topic: True threats as speech outside the guarantee
questions.learningObjective: apply the true-threat category to a face-to-face statement of intent to harm
questions.stem: A man tells a named neighbour, alone on a porch, that he will shoot him next Saturday. How does the law treat that statement, and what must be shown?

As ordinary political protest, because a threat stops being a threat unless the police are also threatened
options.misconception: believes a true threat must include a threat to public officers

options.text: As protected speech, because a true threat is not one unless it names its intended victim in the words spoken
options.misconception: believes a threat is unprotected only if the target is named outright

options.text: As protected speech, because nothing unlawful has happened and the statement may be withdrawn before the day named
options.misconception: believes speech is protected until the threatened act occurs

questions.explanation: A true threat is a serious threat of harm, and it is treated as a category of expression that the constitutional guarantee does not shelter, so the jury may be told that even a single private utterance can be criminal once the prosecution shows the speaker meant it as a threat. The test is about meaning rather than about consequences, so the speaker need not intend to carry the threat out and the listener need not actually fear it. A threat aimed at a private individual is as much within the category as one aimed at the police, and the absence of a stated name is not decisive because context and tone supply what the words do not.

questions.topic: The obscenity test and its elements
questions.learningObjective: name the elements a state must show before restricting an obscene work
questions.stem: A state statute makes it an offence to sell an obscene work. Which set of findings must the state be able to make out before the statute may operate?

options.text: That the work appeals to the prurient interest, describes sexual conduct in an offensive way, and lacks serious value
That the work was first sold and distributed inside the state before any restriction could reach it
options.misconception: believes prior commercial exploitation is one of the required findings

options.text: That an ordinary member of the community would find the work indecent by its own light
options.misconception: believes the ordinary-person finding alone decides the question

options.text: That a majority of the voters in the state would object to the work if it were shown to them
options.misconception: believes local popular objection is one of the required findings

questions.explanation: The conventional definition of obscenity has three parts that must be taken together: a work appeals to the prurient interest of the average person, it describes or depicts sexual conduct in a patently offensive way, and taken as a whole it lacks serious literary, artistic, political, or scientific value. Because the third element operates on the work as a whole, a work may contain offensive passages and still be protected. questions.topic: Time, place, and manner restrictions
questions.learningObjective: state the requirements a content-neutral speech restriction must satisfy
questions.stem: A city bars the handing out of leaflets on its busiest streets, without regard to what any leaflet says or who hands it out. What must the city still be able to show?

options.text: That the bar serves a significant interest, is narrowly drawn to meet it, and still leaves ample ways to reach the audience
Nothing further, because a rule that says nothing about content cannot injure protected speech
options.misconception: believes content neutrality alone defeats every challenge

options.text: The most demanding justification, because a rule about handing out paper is really a rule about the message itself
options.misconception: believes any restriction on a speech channel draws strict scrutiny

options.text: Only that the rule was adopted by a vote of the city council after a public hearing
options.misconception: believes a legislative procedure substitutes for substantive review

Each requirement does a different job: the first identifies what the city is trying to do, the second asks whether a less speech-restrictive rule would serve it, and the third asks whether the audience can still be reached. Content neutrality tells the court which standard to use, not that the rule is automatically sound.

options.misconception: believes the medium of a message settles the analysis

options.text: Neither is reviewable, because sign ordinances fall outside the guarantee that protects speech and press
options.misconception: believes signs and displays sit outside the speech guarantee

options.misconception: believes public land carries no speech interest of its own

options.text: The refusal carries extra weight because the board that made it voted rather than an officer deciding alone
options.misconception: believes a voting procedure settles a speech question

questions.topic: Prior restraint and its presumption
questions.learningObjective: explain why stopping expression in advance is treated more strictly than punishing it afterwards
questions.stem: Before a speech is delivered, a court issues an order forbidding it on the ground that it will break the law. How does that order compare with a punishment imposed after the same speech?

options.text: The order is treated as almost always impermissible, and carries a heavy presumption of invalidity
The order is the ordinary remedy, because preventing harm in advance is always fairer than punishing it later
options.misconception: believes preventing harm always justifies an advance order

options.text: The two are treated alike, because the same words are involved and the same speaker is silenced either way
options.misconception: believes the timing of the order makes no difference

options.text: The order is permitted wherever the speaker has previously broken a law of the same kind
options.misconception: believes a past offence licenses an advance restraint

questions.explanation: An order that stops expression before it happens is treated as the rarest exception, because the objection to a law is normally made afterwards, when the government may point to a concrete harm that actually occurred, and an advance order substitutes the government's forecast for that showing. A later punishment is the ordinary route and is tested on ordinary grounds, and a speaker's earlier misconduct does not by itself authorise a court to silence the next speech in advance.
questions.hint: Ask what the government has to show when it tries to stop words before they are spoken.

questions.topic: The overbreadth doctrine
questions.learningObjective: explain how a court tests a law on its face when it sweeps in protected speech
questions.stem: A law makes it an offence to print any criticism of a named official's record. A publisher challenges the whole statute before a single leaflet has been printed. Which principle lets a court rule on the law as written?

options.text: Overbreadth, which reaches a law that burdens a large amount of protected expression along with its offending part
Vagueness, which requires that ordinary people be able to tell what the statute forbids them to do
options.misconception: believes the challenge turns on what readers can understand

options.text: The political question rule, which lets a court decline an issue committed to another branch of government
options.misconception: believes a court may avoid the question as not its own to decide

options.text: The licensing rule, which requires a permit before any criticism of an official is printed or distributed
options.misconception: believes a permit requirement is the ordinary test for criticism

questions.explanation: A statute that forbids not only the unprotected conduct but a wide field of lawful comment can be struck down in its entirety, because a person who wishes to speak lawfully today cannot be sure the statute will not be read against them tomorrow under some unforeseen application. A law may be perfectly clear and still overbroad, so clarity and reach are two different questions, and the remedy is a narrower statute rather than a licence for a court to rewrite the law itself.

questions.learningObjective: identify the two defects a vague law creates for those subject to it

A prior restraint, because a clause written this broadly will always be used to stop words before they are spoken
options.misconception: believes vagueness is a form of advance restraint

options.text: An improper delegation, because a statute phrased this way hands the decision to a later court
options.misconception: believes an unclear standard is the same as a delegation of lawmaking

options.text: A procedural defect, because no agency could carry out the investigation the clause would require
options.misconception: believes the problem is that the clause cannot be administered in practice

A school may require any expression of loyalty from its pupils for as long as they attend it
options.misconception: believes a school may compel loyalty from children

options.text: A pledge is a promise to say nothing, so a refusal breaks a promise and may be punished as a breach
options.misconception: believes a pledge is a contract rather than an act of expression

options.text: The requirement is lawful whenever most of the pupils in the school would rather salute than not
options.misconception: believes a majority preference licenses a compelled belief

questions.topic: Government speech in its own voice
questions.learningObjective: explain why the speech guarantee does not restrain the government's own message
questions.stem: A government department runs an advertising campaign promoting its own recycling programme and never mentions a neighbouring programme. Is that a difficulty under the speech guarantee?

Yes, because refusing to carry a rival's message is a content-based restriction on that rival's speech
options.misconception: believes silence about a rival is itself a restriction on it

options.text: Yes, because a public department is bound by the same rules of speech as any private advertiser
options.misconception: believes the guarantee binds the government's own voice

options.text: Yes, because an advertisement reaches members of the public who do not work for the department
options.misconception: believes reaching an audience triggers the guarantee

The statute stands, because a flag is the property of the nation and so cannot be an object of speech
options.misconception: believes national property lies outside the speech guarantee

options.text: The statute stands against anyone who acts out of contempt, whatever the political context of the act
options.misconception: believes an intent to insult removes the protection from the conduct

options.text: The statute fails only because the wording is unclear, so the outcome was a technical accident
options.misconception: believes the holding rested on unclear statutory wording

options.misconception: believes school grounds carry no limits beyond those outdoors

It establishes a lawful search, because a resident who answers the door has agreed to be searched

options.misconception: believes permission to enter licenses a search of the whole building

options.misconception: believes informing the driver is the source of the search power

Whether the rifle was suppressed, because anything found in a place is tainted once anything in it is
options.misconception: believes suppression of one item taints every other item automatically

options.text: Whether the officers had probable cause, since that is the only question exclusion ever turns on

options.text: Whether the evidence was helpful to the prosecution, since helpfulness is the only saving consideration
options.misconception: believes helpfulness alone defeats a motion to suppress

questions.topic: Reliance on a defective warrant
questions.learningObjective: explain the good-faith limit on suppression where officers rely on a warrant
questions.stem: A magistrate issues a warrant on an affidavit that a court later finds to rest on a deliberate lie, and the officers search in reliance on the warrant as issued. How does that reliance bear on suppression?

It changes nothing, because any defect later found in an affidavit requires suppression however innocent the officers were
options.misconception: believes officer good faith has no bearing on suppression

options.text: It voids the warrant for good, so a later fresh application on the same facts is equally worthless
options.misconception: believes one defective affidavit taints all later process

options.text: It helps only where the affidavit was in fact accurate, and never where the lie is proved
options.misconception: believes good faith requires a truthful affidavit

options.misconception: believes probable cause is the threshold for an observation

options.misconception: believes the availability of a warrant decides the issue

options.misconception: believes the seriousness of the offence triggers the requirement

options.text: No warning is required, because the requirement reaches only an answer given in writing
options.misconception: believes the requirement is confined to written statements

questions.topic: Testimonial and nontestiminal acts
questions.learningObjective: apply the testimonial test to a spoken account and to a physical sample
questions.stem: A suspect is ordered to give a blood sample and is also asked to describe the scene in his own words. Which of the two does the privilege against self-incrimination protect?

The blood sample, because a needle enters the body and is therefore the greater intrusion
options.misconception: believes physical intrusion is what the test turns on

options.text: Both of them, because any compelled act by a suspect counts as testimony of some kind
options.misconception: believes every compelled act of any sort is testimonial

options.text: Neither of them, because the privilege is only a rule about what a court may admit in evidence
options.misconception: believes the privilege is only an evidentiary rule

How intrusive the procedure feels plays no part in the test, and the privilege is a limit on the government rather than a rule about admissibility at trial.

questions.topic: The grand jury requirement for serious charges
questions.learningObjective: state when a serious charge must come from a grand jury
questions.stem: A person is about to be tried for a serious offence that the federal statutes treat as punishable by a term of more than one year, and the charge has been drawn up as an information rather than an indictment. What does the Fifth Amendment require?

Nothing, because a formal information is itself a charge and satisfies what the text requires
options.misconception: believes an information suffices for a serious offence

options.text: Nothing, because the requirement reaches only a capital offence and not other serious ones
options.misconception: believes the grand jury requirement covers capital cases only

options.text: That the trial judge may substitute a hearing before the court for the finding of the grand jury
options.misconception: believes a judge may stand in for the grand jury

questions.learningObjective: state the test that decides whether two charges are the same offence
questions.stem: A jury acquits a person on a charge. Prosecutors then bring a second case on the same facts charging a different offence that contains every element of the first and adds one more. What decides the claim?

Whether the two offences carry different maximum penalties, since the punishment is what makes a charge distinct
options.misconception: believes the penalty alone distinguishes one offence from another

options.text: Whether the first case ended in an acquittal, because an acquittal bars every later charge on the facts
options.misconception: believes an acquittal bars any second prosecution on the same conduct

options.text: Whether one sovereign prosecutes in each case, since different sovereigns may always be prosecuted twice
options.misconception: believes sovereignty is the decisive test here

He may conduct his own case, because the right to represent oneself knows no limit at all
options.misconception: believes the right of self-representation is unlimited

options.text: He must be left to conduct his own case, because appointing counsel against his will is itself a liberty
options.misconception: believes compulsory counsel infringes the accused's own liberty

options.text: He may conduct his own case if the judge finds the charge simple, since complexity is the decisive factor
options.misconception: believes a judicial assessment of complexity governs the right

questions.topic: Testimonial hearsay and the confrontation right
questions.learningObjective: apply the two requirements for using an absent witness's statement at trial
questions.stem: At a trial, the prosecution offers a witness's earlier written statement to show what she would have said. The accused cannot question her because she has left the country. What does the confrontation guarantee require?

options.text: The statement is testimonial and may not be used, because the accused had no earlier chance to question her
The statement may be used, because a witness who cannot be found could not be questioned in any event
options.misconception: believes unavailability excuses the absence of cross-examination

options.text: The statement may be used, because a statement in writing is never a testimonial statement
options.misconception: believes writing is not a form of testimony for this purpose

options.text: The statement may be used, because a judge may question the witness on the defence's behalf instead
options.misconception: believes a court may substitute its own questioning for cross-examination

questions.topic: Separating devotional provision from compulsory participation

questions.topic: A reported attempt to stop publication
questions.learningObjective: identify the central difficulty with restraining publication in advance
questions.stem: A reader is shown an original summary of a government attempt to stop a newspaper from printing an account of a pending investigation, before the account appears. What is the chief difficulty with that attempt?

It is weak because the investigation is unfinished, since no story is reliable until its subject is settled
options.misconception: believes accuracy is the test applied to a press claim

questions.topic: Why the guarantee protects some speech and not others
questions.learningObjective: explain the categorical scheme for judging speech and defend drawing it by category
questions.stem: Speech receives the strongest protection the law knows when it serves to check and criticise the government, and the least when it amounts to a step towards unlawful conduct. Explain how that difference is drawn, why it is drawn by categories rather than by measuring the harm a case of speech happens to cause, and what follows for a speaker whose message sits close to a boundary.

answer.exemplar: The starting point is that the constitutional guarantee protects the expression of ideas, including ideas that are unpopular, offensive, or wrong, and that the government may not punish a person for the content of a message merely because officials dislike it. The exceptions are therefore drawn narrowly and by category: incitement to imminent lawless action, true threats, fighting words, and obscenity judged against a conventional test, each of which turns on what the expression is rather than on how popular it is. Categories are used because the guarantee is a rule about speech, not a rule about outcomes, and a measure of actual harm would let a government suppress a minority view that had not yet caused harm while permitting a popular view to do damage unchecked, which is the reverse of what the guarantee is for. A speaker near a boundary therefore takes the risk that a court will place the message inside the category, and the practical consequence is that an argument is framed in the strongest terms the speaker can support and is addressed to the audience rather than to the government, because the government is not the forum in which the message can be vindicated.

questions.explanation: A strong answer names the narrow categories that stand outside the guarantee, explains that they are defined by what the expression is rather than by how many people approve of it, and then defends the choice of categories by showing that a harm-based test would produce the wrong result for unpopular speech. It should also say something about the practical consequence for a speaker near a line, since the question asks for that. An answer that lists the categories without explaining why the government may not simply ask whether a message was harmful, or that treats the categories as a list of disfavoured opinions rather than as forms of expression, has missed the reasoning the question is testing.
questions.hint: Answer in three parts: the categories, the reason for using them, and the position of a speaker near a line.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Why a permit scheme and a particular order are different
questions.learningObjective: distinguish a licensing requirement for a category of activity from an order silencing one event
questions.stem: Some cities require a permit before any procession may be held, while a few have tried to stop one particular procession by court order. Explain what makes the two schemes constitutionally different, what a permit scheme must still satisfy, and what a court's order aimed at one event must overcome.

answer.exemplar: A permit scheme is a rule about a category of activity, applied in advance to every procession rather than to a named one, and it therefore does not stop words before they are spoken in the way that a restraint aimed at one event does; a rule of that kind is measured on whether it is drawn on the subject of the message, and a neutral scheme may be sustained if it is reasonably adapted to a significant interest such as traffic, noise, or public order, is drawn no more broadly than that interest requires, and leaves open ample alternative ways for the group to be heard. The defect in a neutral scheme appears when it is administered so that the permission is withheld because of the message, which converts the permit into a licence in fact. An order directed at one named procession is a different thing again, because it picks out a particular expression before the public has heard it, and the objection to stopping expression in advance is far stronger than the objection to punishing it afterwards, so such an order must face a heavy burden and is almost never sustainable. The practical difference is that a city may regulate the manner of processions in advance but may not select which procession survives.

questions.explanation: A strong answer distinguishes a rule about a category from an order about a particular event, explains that a permit scheme is measured by whether it is neutral, adapted to a significant interest, and leaves alternatives open, and then explains that an order aimed at one event is a restraint in advance and must overcome a much heavier burden. It should also note the point at which a permit scheme turns into a licence in fact. An answer that treats both schemes as the same because both are permission, or that describes the permit scheme as unrestricted, has not separated the two questions the item asks about.
questions.hint: Answer in three parts: what the schemes have in common, what a permit rule must show, and what an order against one event must overcome.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Two governments, two doctrines, one structure
questions.learningObjective: synthesise a speech restriction and a compelled affirmation into a single analytical structure
questions.stem: One government bars a person from searching for information about a matter of public concern while inside a public building. A second requires that person to state aloud what he believes before it will issue him a permit. Using the doctrines rather than the names of the parties, explain the structure the two measures share, what each doctrine asks of the government, and why one measure is far easier to defend than the other.

answer.exemplar: The shared structure is that each government has attached a condition to a person's access to an activity or a place, and each has turned the person's own judgment into the price of admission: the first condition is a rule about what may be looked for in a public building, and the second is a rule about what must be said before a permit issues. The doctrines are, first, that the guarantee protects a person against being made to speak, and second, that it protects a person against being told what he may look for or say, together with the rule that a restriction drawn on the subject of a message faces the demanding standard while one drawn only on the manner of doing something faces the middle standard. The second measure is the harder to defend by a wide margin, because compelling a person to declare a belief is the most direct possible interference with the freedom to hold and express an opinion, and no showing of administrative convenience has been accepted as a justification for it. The first measure may well be sustained, because a rule that keeps a person from conducting a search inside a public building can be defended as a limit on the use of the building rather than as a limit on the person's opinion, provided it applies whatever the subject of the search and leaves other ways of obtaining the same information open. The contrast shows why the same government sometimes wins and sometimes loses on what looks like the same requirement of neutrality.

questions.explanation: A strong answer identifies the common structure, names each doctrine and the question each asks of the government, and then explains why one measure survives and the other does not, referring to the demanding standard and to the directness of the interference. It should avoid arguing only from the labels of the parties and should make clear which feature of each measure carries the weight. An answer that says one measure is unconstitutional and stops there, or that treats the two as unrelated because the governments differ, has not done the comparison the item sets.
questions.hint: Start with the shared structure, name the two doctrines, and then say which feature of each measure decides the outcome.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The order of steps in a speech challenge
questions.learningObjective: correct a misplaced arrow in a diagram of the speech analysis
questions.stem: A diagram of a speech challenge shows five boxes joined by arrows. The boxes are: identify what the speaker claims; decide whether the rule is drawn on the content of the message; identify the place involved; apply the standard of review; decide the case. The arrows as drawn run from claims to content, from claims to place, from content to the standard, and from the standard to the outcome. One arrow is drawn in the wrong place. Which arrow is misplaced, and what is the correct order for the two boxes it connects?

options.text: The arrow from claims to place, because the place is settled before the character of the rule is examined
The arrow from claims to content, because the character of the rule is settled before the claim is identified
options.misconception: believes the claim comes after the rule is classified

options.text: The arrow from content to the standard, because the standard is applied only after the case has been decided
options.misconception: believes the standard follows the outcome

options.text: The arrow from the standard to the outcome, because the case is decided before any standard is applied
options.misconception: believes the outcome precedes the standard

questions.explanation: A court works from the outside in: it first settles whether the speaker is protected at all, then identifies the place, because what a government may do depends heavily on whether the place is a street or a room it controls, and only then does it characterise the rule as drawn on content or on delivery, since the character of the rule selects the standard, which is applied last before the case is decided. The misplaced arrow is the one running straight from the claim to the content question, because it allows the character of the rule to be examined before the place is known, and a rule can be content-neutral in a place the government controls and content-based in a place it has opened to the public. The other three arrows are in the right order.
questions.hint: Ask which of the two classifications depends on the other, and follow the arrow that skips a step.
